Random effects, and mixed models

DSCI 632: Statistics for Data Science

Peter Ralph

Random effects

An example: sleep

From Belenky et al, Patterns of performance degradation and restoration during sleep restriction and subsequent recovery: a sleep dose-response study (and included in the lme4 package).

The average reaction time per day (in milliseconds) for subjects in a sleep deprivation study. These data are from the study described in Belenky et al. (2003), for the most sleep-deprived group (3 hours time-in-bed) and for the first 10 days of the study, up to the recovery period.

library(lme4)
head(sleepstudy)
##   Reaction Days Subject

## 2 258.7047    1     308
## 3 250.8006    2     308

## 5 356.8519    4     308
## 6 414.6901    5     308

sleepstudy |> ggplot(aes(x=Days, y=Reaction)) +
    geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm", formula=y~x) +

First pass: lm()

lm1 <- lm(Reaction ~ Days, data=sleepstudy)
summary(lm1)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = Reaction ~ Days, data = sleepstudy)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -110.848  -27.483    1.546   26.142  139.953

How’d that work?

Reaction ~ Days
sleep <- sleepstudy |> mutate( lm1 = predict(lm1, newdata=sleepstudy) )
sleep |> pivot_longer(cols=c(Reaction, lm1), values_to="Reaction", names_to="what") |>
    mutate(what=fct_recode(what, data="Reaction")) |>
    ggplot(aes(x=Days, y=Reaction, color=what)) +
    geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm", formula=y~x) +
    facet_wrap(~ Subject, nrow=2)

Critique:

That single line more or less summarizes how much reaction time goes up per night.

After all, it’s what we’d get if we ignored Subject.

But, this is wrong!

sleep |> ggplot(aes(x=Days, y=Reaction)) +
    geom_point(aes(color=Subject)) + geom_smooth(method="lm", formula=y~x)

xkcd:2533

A reminder: “the” linear model

lm(Reaction ~ Days)

fits the model (\(R_i\) and \(D_i\) are the \(i^\text{th}\) Reaction and Days entries) \[\begin{aligned} R_i &= b_0 + b_{\text{Days}} \times D_i + \epsilon_i \\ \epsilon_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\text{mean}=0, \text{sd}=\sigma) , \end{aligned}\] where the \(\epsilon_i\) are independent.

This means that we’ll be wrong: overconfident about the estimate.

Separate lines per subject?

lm2 <- lm(Reaction ~ Days * Subject, data=sleepstudy)
summary(lm2)

Reaction ~ Days * Subject
sleep <- sleep |> mutate( lm2 = predict(lm2, newdata=sleepstudy) )
sleep |> pivot_longer(cols=c(Reaction, lm2, lm1), values_to="Reaction", names_to="what") |>
    mutate(what=fct_recode(what, data="Reaction")) |>
    ggplot(aes(x=Days, y=Reaction, color=what)) +
    geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm", formula=y~x) +
    facet_wrap(~ Subject, nrow=2)

What’d we do there?

lm(Reaction ~ Days * Subject)

fits the model (\(R_i\), \(D_i\) and \(S_i\) are the \(i^\text{th}\) Reaction, Days, and Subject entries) \[\begin{aligned} R_{i} &= b_{S_i,0} + b_{S_i,\text{Days}} \times D_i + \epsilon_i \\ \epsilon_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\text{mean}=0, \text{sd}=\sigma) . \end{aligned}\] The \(\epsilon_i\) are still independent, but there’s a different slope and intercept for each subject.

But we wanted to know the overall effect!

Random effects

Here’s one approach: \[\begin{aligned} R_{i} &= b_0 + b_\text{Days} \times D_i + b_{S_i,0} + b_{S_i,\text{Days}} \times D_i + \epsilon_i \\ \epsilon_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\text{mean}=0, \text{sd}=\sigma) \\ b_{S_i,0} &\sim \text{Normal}(\text{mean}=0, \text{sd}=\eta) \\ b_{S_i,\text{Days}} &\sim \text{Normal}(\text{mean}=0, \text{sd}=\eta) \\ \end{aligned}\] We’re allowing subject-specific deviations from a common slope and intercept.

lme4::lmer

This has random intercepts and slopes by subject:

fm1 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Subject), data=sleepstudy)
summary(fm1)
## Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod']
## Formula: Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Subject)
##    Data: sleepstudy
## 
## REML criterion at convergence: 1743.6
## 
## Scaled residuals: 
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -3.9536 -0.4634  0.0231  0.4634  5.1793 
## 
## Random effects:
##  Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev. Corr 
##  Subject  (Intercept) 612.10   24.741        
##           Days         35.07    5.922   0.07 
##  Residual             654.94   25.592        
## Number of obs: 180, groups:  Subject, 18
## 
## Fixed effects:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value
## (Intercept)  251.405      6.825  36.838
## Days          10.467      1.546   6.771
## 
## Correlation of Fixed Effects:
##      (Intr)
## Days -0.138

Here are the estimated random effects themselves:

rf1 <- ranef(fm1) |> as.data.frame()
rf1 |> ggplot(aes(y=grp, x=condval)) +
    geom_point() + facet_wrap(~term, scales="free_x") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin=condval -2*condsd,
                      xmax=condval +2*condsd), width=0) +
    labs(x="coefficent", y="subject")

And, the per-subject results:

sleep <- sleep |> mutate(
    rf1 = predict(fm1, newdata=sleepstudy)
)
sleep |> pivot_longer(cols=c(Reaction, lm2, lm1, rf1), values_to="Reaction", names_to="what") |>
    mutate(what=fct_recode(what, data="Reaction")) |>
    ggplot(aes(x=Days, y=Reaction, color=what)) +
    geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm", formula=y~x) +
    geom_abline(slope=fixef(fm1)["Days"], intercept=fixef(fm1)["(Intercept)"]) +
    facet_wrap(~ Subject, nrow=2)

Another example: urchins

An example: urchins eat algae

From Logan:

To investigate density-dependent grazing effects of sea urchin Andrew and Underwood (1993) on filamentous algae measured the percentage of filamentous algae within five quadrats randomly positioned within each of four random patches of reef that were in turn nested within four sea urchin density treatments (no urchins, 33% of natural density, 66% natural density and 100% natural density). The sea urchin density treatment was considered a fixed factor and patch within density treatment as well as the individual quadrats were treated as random factors.

An example: urchins eat algae

andrew_data <- read.table('../datasets/Logan_data/andrew.tsv', header=T, sep='\t')
head(andrew_data)
##   TREAT PATCH QUAD ALGAE
## 1    0%     1    1    46
## 2    0%     1    2    44
## 3    0%     1    3    41
## 4    0%     1    4    29
## 5    0%     1    5    11
## 6    0%     2    1    65

There are four variables: TREAT, PATCH, QUAD and ALGAE

Main effect factor: TREAT

Both QUAD and PATCH are factors:

andrew_data$QUAD <- factor(andrew_data$QUAD)
andrew_data$PATCH <- factor(andrew_data$PATCH)
andrew_data$TREAT <- factor(andrew_data$TREAT, levels=c("0%", "33%", "66%", "100%"))

Response distribution

andrew_data |> mutate(patch_num=factor(as.numeric(PATCH)%%4)) |> 
    ggplot(aes(x=TREAT, y=ALGAE)) + geom_boxplot() +
    geom_jitter(aes(color=patch_num))

Why is this wrong?

summary(lm(ALGAE ~ TREAT, data=andrew_data))

##    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max

What we really want: \[ \text{(algae)} = \text{(mean for treatment)} + \text{(mean offset for patch)} + \text{("noise")} . \]

We could do:

ALGAE ~ TREAT + PATCH

… but do we care about all those patch means?

Random effects

Small modification: \[ \text{(algae)} = \text{(mean for treatment)} + \text{(random offset for patch)} + \text{("noise")} . \]

We add a random intercept:

ALGAE ~ TREAT + (1|PATCH)

library(lme4)
alglm <- lmer(ALGAE ~ TREAT + (1|PATCH), data=andrew_data)
summary(alglm)

##  PATCH    (Intercept) 294.3    17.16   
##  Residual             298.6    17.28   
## Number of obs: 80, groups:  PATCH, 16
## 
## Fixed effects:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value
## (Intercept)   39.200      9.408   4.167
## TREAT33%     -20.200     13.305  -1.518
## TREAT66%     -17.650     13.305  -1.327
## TREAT100%    -37.900     13.305  -2.849

Notes on mixed models

The math is a lot harder.

For a simple linear model fit by lm( ) (with fixed effects), the log-likelihood function is just the sum of the squared residuals.

But with a mixed model, the likelihood averages over the values of the random effects, which makes everything more difficult.

You sometimes have to worry about convergence.

Since the math is harder, mixed-model-fitting functions like lmer( ) have to use various sorts of numerical optimization methods to find the best-fitting parameters.

Sometimes, these may fail.

Notably, many use the REML approximation:

Usage:

     lmer(formula, data = NULL, REML = TRUE, control = lmerControl(),
          start = NULL, verbose = 0L, subset, weights, na.action,
          offset, contrasts = NULL, devFunOnly = FALSE, ...)

Hypothesis testing?

With fixed effects, for a factor f, the comparison

anova( lm(y ~ f - 1), lm(y ~ 1) )

uses the model that \[ y_i = \beta_{f_i} + \epsilon_i \] to test against the null hypothesis that \[ H_0 : \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \cdots = \beta_m = 0. \]

With random effects,

anova( lm(y ~ (1|f) - 1), lm(y ~ 1) )

uses the model that \[\begin{aligned} y_i &= \beta_{f_i} + \epsilon_i \\ \beta_a &\sim \Normal(0, \eta) \end{aligned}\] to test against the null hypothesis that \[ H_0 : \eta = 0. \]

Back to the pumpkins

Your turn

  1. Adjust the simulations so that there is an effect of plot, drawn randomly from Normal(0, 1).
  2. Fit a model including a random effect for plot.
  3. How big is the “plot” effect? Is it estimated correctly?
  4. Assess significance by using anova( ) to compare to a nested model.

Simulate data

(Here’s our previous code:)

pumpkins <- expand.grid(
          fertilizer=c("low", "medium", "high"),
          water=c("no water", "water"),
          plot=1:4,
          plant=1:5,
          weight=NA)

params <- list(
    mu = 5, # all units are kg
    alpha = c(low=0, medium=2, high=4),
    beta = c("no water"=0, water=1),
    sigma = 1
)
params$gamma <- rep(0, 6)
names(params$gamma) <- outer(c("low", "medium", "high"), c("no water", "water"), paste, sep=",")
params$gamma["high,water"] <-  5

pumpkins$condition <- paste(pumpkins$fertilizer, pumpkins$water, sep=",")
pumpkins$mean_weight <-
    params$mu +
    params$alpha[pumpkins$fertilizer] +
    params$beta[pumpkins$water] +
    params$gamma[pumpkins$condition]

set.seed(123)
pumpkins$weight <- rnorm(nrow(pumpkins), mean=pumpkins$mean_weight, sd=params$sigma)
